hypotheses.name: Abstract-noun ballast
hypotheses.claim: AI-drafted passages carry roughly 5x the density of three-item abstract coordinations ("agile, resilient, and able to respond"; "clarity, discipline, and results"; "flexibility, clarity, and confidence") and ~1.5x the density of nominalisations, and they let abstractions occupy the grammatical subject slot ("Oversight should guide, not micromanage." "Accountability matters." "Administration is not inherently negative..."). Human passages of the same detector score enumerate countable things instead, and their subjects are people, bodies, or objects with names. Measured: triads 0.70/100w AI vs 0.13 human; -tion/-ment/-ance/-ence/-ility tokens 4.18% vs 2.89%. Falsifiable: if human speeches at these scores were equally triad-dense, the feature is worthless.
hypotheses.how: Cap `X, Y, and Z` coordinations at one per 300 words. Where you want a list, make it 4-6 countable items of mixed grain and end it on the outlier, not the grandest member -- human models are "three physicians, a licenced practical nurse, a nurse practitioner, and a social worker" and "Ontario, British Columbia, Nova Scotia, and even as far as Argentina", not "prevention, treatment, recovery, and harm reduction". Then scan every sentence's subject: if it is an -ion/-ment/-ity noun (oversight, accountability, administration, transparency), rewrite so the subject is a person, a named body, or a physical thing that acts.

hypotheses.name: Cadence floor
hypotheses.claim: The AI passages run a longer mean sentence (20.4 words vs 16.8) with LOWER relative variance (CV 0.47 vs 0.55) and 30% more commas per word (7.19 vs 5.49) -- the extra commas are appositives and triads, i.e. the machine lengthens by packing modifiers into a stable 18-25 word frame rather than by alternating lengths. Humans drop to 2-6 word sentences mid-argument ("This is serious." "That's what is needed." "I have highlighted that." "I don't know." "Absolutely.").
hypotheses.how: Target mean 16-17 words with a standard deviation of at least 9. Concretely: for every 100 words, land at least one sentence of 6 words or fewer that is a bare assertion or reaction (not "Thank you, Madam Speaker"), and at least one of 30+. Do the lengthening by adding a whole clause or a following sentence, not by adding an appositive -- if a sentence has three or more commas that are not separating list items, split it.

hypotheses.name: Announced verbatim repetition
hypotheses.claim: Both sides repeat themselves, but differently. Humans repeat the SAME WORDS and flag it: "we matched 15 000 people with these clinics -- I repeat, 15 000 people"; "I'm going to say that one more time: Public confidence is built when the public can access health care"; "I want to say that again"; "we cannot -- we cannot --". AI restates the same proposition with synonyms and no marker: "families who have carried the burden of separation and grief... the veterans who have returned home changed by their service" followed one sentence later by "families who carry the burden of separation and loss and the veterans who returned home forever changed by their service"; "the Mactaquac Life Achievement Project is a bold and necessary investment in our energy future. The bill ensures..." followed by the same sentence with "This legislation ensures". Repetition markers appear in 15% of human segments and 2% of AI ones.
hypotheses.how: When you repeat a point, repeat the exact clause, unchanged, and announce it: "I repeat", "I will say that again", or the doubled phrase inside dashes. Then run the inverse check: find any two sentences in the draft that assert the same thing with different vocabulary, and either delete one or collapse them into one verbatim-repeated clause. Silent synonym-swapped restatement is the single most reliable machine tell here.

hypotheses.name: Numbers with a baseline and an attributor
hypotheses.claim: Human passages carry 2.4x the digit density (1.48% of tokens vs 0.63%) and 9x the rate of comparison anchors (0.46/100w vs 0.05). Human numbers almost always arrive with a prior value, a rank, or a named source: "downgraded Foundever Group to a CCC rating from a previous B-"; "Thirty-four percent... up from 28% just last fall"; "Canada's household debt is around 100% to 101% of GDP, the United Kingdom comes in second at 76%"; "798 permanent registered nurses... Between April 2023 and March 31, 2024"; "an undefeated 11-0-1 record". AI numbers are round, solitary and uncompared: "$5 million", "a new 50-bed addiction treatment facility", "tens of millions of dollars", "10 newly established trainer positions".
hypotheses.how: Give every number a second number or a named issuer. Never let a figure stand alone: pair it with what it was before, where it ranks, or who published it. Prefer ragged precision to round precision ("100% to 101%", "68% to 69%", "April 2023 to March 31, 2024" -- note the mismatched endpoint precision) and let at least one figure be an unimportant one that no argument rests on.

hypotheses.name: Unanswered question runs
hypotheses.claim: Humans ask 4x as many questions (8.1% of sentences vs 2.1%) and ask them in runs of short separate sentences that go unanswered or get a one-word answer: "Is this the right process? Is this the right makeup of the complaint committee? I don't know."; "What specific problems exist under the current framework?... What safeguards against misuse exist? What independent oversight mechanisms are in place? Those answers are not clearly provided in this bill."; "Can we do better? Absolutely. Again, it comes down to how. How do we do it?". The AI's one question is a colon-introduced stack of interrogative phrases inside a single sentence -- "We must ask: What information could be withheld, from whom, under what safeguards, and with what appeal mechanisms?" -- and it is immediately dissolved by a balancing maxim ("Transparency and confidentiality must be balanced carefully").
hypotheses.how: Ask 3-5 questions as separate short sentences in a row, addressed to a specific person or body who could answer them. Do not answer them yourself; close the run with a flat non-answer ("I don't know", "Those answers are not clearly provided in this bill", "Is that the answer?"). Never write a question as a colon plus a comma-stacked list of interrogatives, and never follow a question with a symmetrical both-sides sentence.

hypotheses.name: Self-limiting first person
hypotheses.claim: Human text concedes about the SPEAKER; AI text concedes only about the world. Zero of 40 AI seeds contain a self-limiting marker; 15% of human exemplars do -- "Honestly, I'm not an expert in social work or addiction treatment"; "I don't know"; "If I read the tea leaves a little bit"; "not to sound harsh, but"; "I don't think that's a complete sentence in and of itself". The AI concession template is world-facing and three-beat: assert, concede, reverse ("Accountability matters. However, centralization also carries risks." / "There is merit to that argument... However, overriding existing privacy legislation certainly demands rigorous justification."), and what follows the reversal is another abstraction. Humans follow a concession with an instance: "there are still real challenges... Weather can intervene. Sometimes, when I've ordered stuff, it takes time for it to get in, and the patient is not available." Human I/my/me density is 1.28% vs 0.57%; 10% of human sentences open with I/Well/So/But/Now vs 3.6%.
hypotheses.how: Include at least one admission about your own knowledge or position -- what you don't know, haven't read, aren't expert in, or got wrong. Delete every assert/however/reverse triple whose reversal lands on another abstract noun; where you keep a concession, the very next sentence must be a specific instance with a date, place, or object. Open roughly one sentence in ten with I, Well, So, But, or Now.

hypotheses.name: Room deixis and disputed wording
hypotheses.claim: Human passages are not fully readable without the room: they cite what another member just said and quarrel over exact language -- "the opposition proposed a subamendment to remove the words 'to continue' from our amendment"; "My colleague has referred to the fact that babies are being born on the side of the highway. I've heard it mentioned a few times."; "As the member opposite suggested"; "I clearly said I didn't want an answer about the school lunch program"; "There are a lot of people on this side who are seniors, and there are a few on the other side"; and they carry executed procedure verbatim ("(Bill 21, An Act to Amend the Child and Youth Well-Being Act, was read a third time and passed.)", "resolve itself into the Committee of Supply to open and set aside the capital estimates"). AI text is self-contained: it gestures at procedure in the abstract ("This clause deserves detailed committee scrutiny", "When the bill goes to the committee") and never quotes another speaker or a contested phrase. Procedure idiom appears in 23% of human segments vs 10% of AI.
hypotheses.how: Put in one reference to a specific thing said earlier by a positioned other (the member opposite, my colleague, the minister), reported closely enough that you could be contradicted. Quote the exact words under dispute in quotation marks. Name procedural objects at full specificity -- bill number plus long title, the committee's proper name, the stage -- rather than saying "committee" or "this legislation".

hypotheses.name: Gloss discipline
hypotheses.claim: AI drafts define what they name; humans drop a reference and move on. AI: "community economic development corporations. These organizations allow residents to invest directly in businesses by purchasing community investment shares"; the full expansion of the PACE program; "Alex in this story". Humans leave the load-bearing reference unexplained -- "We saw what happened in Moncton last year." is followed by one clause and then dropped; "Motion 4", "Nursing Home Without Walls and others", "the 17 by Seventeen challenge", "Foundever", "Wela'lin" all arrive without apposition. Where a human does gloss, the gloss adds a dated external fact ("recognized as a top nation-building project last November"), not a definition.
hypotheses.how: Pick two named entities in the draft and delete their explanatory appositive entirely -- let the name stand alone. Allow yourself one gloss, and make it a dated event or a comparison rather than a definition of the category. Also include at least one proper noun that carries no argumentative weight (a lake, a dog's name, a second piece of equipment, the exact award category) -- humans name incidentals, machines name only what the passage is about.

hypotheses.name: Descending ending
hypotheses.claim: AI passages end by climbing back to the opening thesis or up to a province-wide abstraction: the 88-scoring seed's last sentence is a near-verbatim echo of its fifth ("our public health system is agile, resilient, and able to respond to new and emerging threats"); another closes "Otherwise, we risk adding weight to a system already struggling under operational strain"; another "a practical and necessary step, and one that reflects the kind of balance we should strive for in our labour standards." Human passages end smaller and unresolved, often on a person or a concrete image, sometimes on an aside: "He will forever be one of my favourite blueberry pie social dates. Rest in peace, my friend Dan."; "Those answers are not clearly provided in this bill."; "I could have my baby on the side of the Trans-Canada Highway because I won't have time to get to another facility."; "I want people to continue to be encouraged."; "The numbers drop from there."
hypotheses.how: Compare the abstraction level of your last sentence to your first. If the last is broader, rewrite it. End on something narrower than anything else in the passage -- one named person, one object, one unresolved question, or a flat deflation ("The numbers drop from there", "It's the evolution of time") -- and never let the closing sentence share more than a couple of content words with the opening thesis.
